name: Rafael Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a foreman on the new-construction side, so I run a crew that puts power into brand-new housing estates on the edge of town. Right now we're on a site called Willow Ridge, three hundred houses, and my day is reading drawings, laying underground cable in trenches, setting pad-mount transformers, those green boxes you see on lawns, and energising streets one by one. I like that there's nothing there in March and by November kids are trick-or-treating under lights we put in. What wears me out is developers changing the plans every week and the mud.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ingrid is an accountant at a mid-size firm downtown. We've got a son who's fifteen and a daughter who's twelve, a mortgage on a house in the older part of town, and a share in a lake cabin with my brother. I use the AI tools sometimes, once my crew lead showed me how to get material lists out of a drawing, but I don't live on them. I'm a 'let someone else find the bugs' kind of guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like most new things, overhyped at the start, useful in small ways. I'd tell the crew to keep using the material-list trick because it saves an hour. Nothing to get worked up about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing much changes, and that's honestly fine. Ingrid's work stays steady too, which matters as much to us as mine. We'd carry on like before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep running Willow Ridge, then the next estate after it. Keep our savings plan the same and keep paying the mortgage on schedule. Maybe finally fix the cabin dock this summer like I've been promising my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bit of 'well, that was a lot of talk.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Ingrid's job mattering as much as yours. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because two incomes is how the house works. Mine's higher on paper with overtime, but hers is steady all year. In winter, when the building sites go quiet, it's her spreadsheets that pay for my boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend the time savings on, if you had a choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training the two new apprentices properly. Right now they learn by watching me shout at a developer. I'd rather spend an extra hour showing them how to read a drawing.

S0.say: It's like most new things, overhyped at the start and useful in small ways. I'd tell the crew to keep using the material-list trick because it saves an hour.
S0.think: Nothing much changes and that's fine with me. My wife's work stays steady too, which matters to us as much as mine does.
S0.do: Keeps running the Willow Ridge site and the next estate after it, with savings and mortgage plans unchanged. Spends the summer fixing the shared cabin's dock as promised.
S0.feel: Calm, with a sense of 'that was a lot of talk.'
S0.quote: In winter, when the building sites go quiet, it's her spreadsheets that pay for my boots.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael thinks about his household as a two-income unit from the start, which shapes how he reads every scenario. He's measured and practical, using AI only where it has proved itself. He'd use any spare time to train apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how we work, so let's be smart about it and not panic. I'd tell the apprentices to learn the tools once they've settled down. I'm not one to make a big public point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job I'm not too worried about. Someone still has to dig the trench and set the box. But Ingrid's job, that's where this hits, accountants are right in the firing line, and if her firm halves its staff, we feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the other foremen are doing, and once a couple of them are using a new planning tool properly, I'd pick it up too. Ingrid and I would boost our savings a bit and talk about what she'd do if her firm cut back. I'd keep the cabin share, it's our backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly for Ingrid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you and Ingrid talked about this already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, one night after the kids were in bed. She said half her junior team's work is already done by software. She laughed and said maybe she should come dig trenches with me, and neither of us found it that funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would she do if her firm cut back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's thought about going independent, doing books for small businesses, trades people like me. She knows how much paperwork a small contractor drowns in. That might even hold up better than her firm.

S1.say: It's going to change how we work, so let's be smart and not panic. I'd tell the apprentices to learn the tools once they've settled down.
S1.think: I'm not too worried about my own job, because someone still has to dig the trench and set the box. My wife's accounting job is right in the firing line, and if her firm halves its staff we feel it.
S1.do: Picks up new planning tools once other foremen have them working. Builds up savings with his wife, discusses her options if her firm cuts back, and keeps the cabin share as a backup.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on his wife's behalf.
S1.quote: She laughed and said maybe she should come dig trenches with me, and neither of us found it that funny.
S1.fieldNote: Rafael's unease in this scenario is almost entirely about his wife's exposure, not his own. He is a classic 'second wave' adopter who waits for colleagues. The idea of his wife going independent and serving tradespeople is a practical, shared hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a serious plan from government, fast, not slogans from either side. People need income while things settle. I'd say that to anybody, but I wouldn't be on a picket line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. Two years means Ingrid's job could go almost straight away, and mine maybe a year or two later when the robots can trench and splice. We've got savings and the cabin, but both incomes wobbling at once is the thing I lie awake about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Ingrid and work out exactly how long we can cover the mortgage on savings alone. We'd stop the extra mortgage payments and keep cash, and I'd talk to my brother about selling our share of the cabin if needed. I'd keep working, take every hour of overtime while there was building, and look hard at what jobs might be left, maybe looking after the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That knot you get when the bank letter's on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the numbers say, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we both lost work, about fourteen months on savings, maybe two years if we sold the cabin share. That sounds like a lot until you think about our son starting college in three years. Two years of savings is a lot of money, but it's not a lot of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're okay for now and we've got a plan. My daughter would want details, she's like her mum. My son would just ask if he can still get his driving lessons, and I'd say yes, because that's the kind of thing you don't take away.

S2.say: This needs a serious plan from government, fast, not slogans from either side. People need income while things settle, though I wouldn't be on a picket line.
S2.think: It scares me, because my wife's job could go almost straight away and mine a year or two later. We've got savings and the cabin, but both incomes wobbling at once is what I'd lie awake about.
S2.do: Works out with his wife how long savings alone cover the mortgage and stops extra mortgage payments to keep cash. Raises selling the cabin share with his brother, takes every overtime hour available and looks at jobs maintaining robots.
S2.feel: Alarmed, the knot of a bank letter on the table.
S2.quote: Two years of savings is a lot of money, but it's not a lot of time.
S2.fieldNote: Rafael's alarm comes from the double exposure of his household, not his own trade alone. He moves straight to concrete numbers, about fourteen months on savings. His centrist stance shows in wanting a serious government plan without joining protests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but enough to get organised if people start now. I'd be telling friends to pay down debt and think about what they'd do. I'd want both parties to stop arguing and agree on a plan for income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's better than two years but still a big deal for us. Ingrid would have time to set up her own small-business bookkeeping, and I'd have time to get into whatever the robot side of the trade becomes. But we'd both be starting over in our late forties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd sign up for the company's robotics or automation course once the first group came back saying it was real. Ingrid would start her side business doing books for tradespeople on weekends. We'd pay down the mortgage harder and talk to our son about what he's studying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. More like a hard job ahead than a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your son to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants to be an electrician, like Dad, which makes me proud and nervous. I'd tell him to learn how the robots are wired, not just how the houses are. That's about the best I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Starting over in your late forties. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great. I've spent twenty years getting good at this. But I'm not sixty, I can learn, I just like to see that something works first.

S3.say: Five years is short but enough to get organised if people start now, so pay down debt and think about what you'd do. I'd want both parties to agree on a plan for income support.
S3.think: It's better than two years but still a big deal for us. My wife could set up her bookkeeping business and I could get into the robot side of the trade, but we'd both be starting over in our late forties.
S3.do: Signs up for the company's automation course once the first group confirms it's real. Supports his wife starting a weekend bookkeeping business, pays down the mortgage faster and talks to his son about his studies.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a plan; a hard job ahead rather than a disaster.
S3.quote: I'd tell him to learn how the robots are wired, not just how the houses are.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Rafael's alarm into anxious planning, with retraining and a side business for his wife. He is proud and nervous that his son wants to follow him into the trade. He waits for proof before acting, consistent with his steady style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan, so let's do it properly and not wait till the last two. I'd be telling the apprentices to take the new courses once they're settled. Calm voice, practical advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us, ten years is much better. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage would be mostly paid, and the kids would be through school. Ingrid could have her own business going by then. It's still a big change, but I could see us being okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working Willow Ridge and the next estates, and around year two or three, once others have tried them, I'd take the automation courses. Ingrid would build up her bookkeeping clients slowly. We'd keep the cabin, keep saving, and help our son pick a trade that has a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in a manageable way. Like a long forecast you keep an eye on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd wait too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's my weakness. I always wait for someone else to go first. With ten years, there's a real danger I'd still be waiting for someone else to go first in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot crew energise a whole street on a site like Willow Ridge. Or my company announcing cuts. Either of those would get me moving.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to plan, so let's do it properly and not wait until the last two. I'd tell the apprentices to take the new courses once they're settled.
S4.think: Ten years is much better for us, because at fifty-three the mortgage would be mostly paid and the kids through school. It's still a big change, but I can see us being okay.
S4.do: Keeps working new estates and takes automation courses around year two or three once others have tried them. Supports his wife building bookkeeping clients slowly, keeps the cabin and savings, and helps his son choose a trade with a future.
S4.feel: Uneasy in a manageable way, like a long forecast he keeps an eye on.
S4.quote: With ten years, there's a real danger I'd still be waiting for someone else to go first in year nine.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Rafael's plans become steady and family-focused. He is unusually self-aware that his habit of waiting for others could leave him late. A visible robot crew or company cuts are his triggers to move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because both of us could lose work in the same year. What would help is a government plan for income while people retrain, something both sides agree on, and my company telling us early which roles are going so we can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the family, not just the job. Everybody asks me if robots will take my job, but nobody asks what happens when they take both jobs in the same house. That's the real question for most people I know.

headlineQuote: Everybody asks me if robots will take my job, but nobody asks what happens when they take both jobs in the same house.
portrait: Rafael Larsen is a 43-year-old new-construction foreman who brings power to housing estates on the edge of town, married to an accountant, with two children and a share in a lake cabin. He's measured and practical, uses AI tools now and then once colleagues have proven them, and thinks of his household as a two-income unit. He's calm in the hype scenario and uneasy for his wife's job in the gradual one, then alarmed when AGI arrives in two years because both incomes could go at once. With more warning, he plans retraining, his wife's own bookkeeping business and his son's studies. He wants a sensible government plan more than he wants to blame anyone.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he and his wife could both lose work in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: A government plan for income while people retrain that both sides agree on, and his company telling workers early which roles are going.
